title: Bell and Smile
premise: Folklorist Lior Crane arrives in the hollow of Ashen Bell to record a dying song tradition, armed with tape reels and a rationalist's contempt for the villagers' refusal to sing any verse twice. His overnight sleep recordings begin capturing a second voice that answers his questions, and he learns the village survives by an ancient count: every household must surrender one member when the bell tolls, and outsiders who hear the second voice are counted as family. As Lior's recordings unravel the entity's true name, he must smuggle the widow Merrin Hale and her daughter out before the next tolling—only to discover the count can be satisfied by whoever answers last. In the end Lior gives his own voice to the bell, buying the Hales their escape while his tapes, playing back in an empty house, keep asking questions no one answers.
about_author: Wren Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist of regional oral histories who spent three years collecting lullabies in remote farming communities before turning to fiction. They live near the coast, where they still refuse to hum along to songs they don't know all the words to.

chapters.title: The Road That Forgets Its Name
chapters.summary: Lior Crane arrives in Ashen Bell by bus, cataloguing the village's silence for his field notes. Third-person limited from Lior's POV. The emotional beat is smug curiosity: he sees superstition where the reader will learn to see survival.

chapters.title: A Room Above the Smithy
chapters.summary: Lior lodges with Merrin Hale and her daughter Iva, the only household willing to take him. He notices salt lines under doors and nails driven outward at window frames. POV: Lior. The beat is unease disguised as anthropological interest.

chapters.title: Songs Sung Once
chapters.summary: At the tavern, Lior coaxes old Tam Voss into singing the harvest verse; the room empties mid-song. Tam warns him never to ask for it twice. POV: Lior. The beat is the first crack in his certainty—he wants the second verse more than he wants to be safe.

chapters.title: What the Reels Keep
chapters.summary: Lior sets his recorder running overnight to capture ambient sound. Reviewing the tape, he hears breathing that isn't his, and a question posed softly in his own cadence. POV: Lior. The beat is denial curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: Iva Counts the Doors
chapters.summary: Eight-year-old Iva tells Lior there are forty-one houses but only forty names on the church roll, and that the missing name 'walks at counting time.' POV shifts to Iva. The beat is childlike matter-of-factness that makes the horror land harder.

chapters.title: The Widow's Bargain
chapters.summary: Merrin admits her husband was taken by the last count and begs Lior to leave before the autumn tolling. She reveals hearing the second voice marks you as kin. POV: Merrin. The beat is protective desperation meeting Lior's stubbornness.

chapters.title: Questions Answered
chapters.summary: Lior deliberately speaks into the recorder at night: 'Who are you?' The second voice replies with his childhood address. POV: Lior. The beat is terror wearing the mask of scientific triumph—he transcribes everything.

chapters.title: Forty Names, Forty-One Houses
chapters.summary: Lior cross-references parish records and finds a name scraped off every fifty years, always after a tolling. The village has been paying something for two centuries. POV: Lior. The beat is the historian's vertigo of finding the pattern.

chapters.title: Tam's Last Verse
chapters.summary: Drunk and grieving, Tam sings the forbidden second verse as a warning: the bell counts voices, not bodies. By morning Tam is gone and the bell has a new tone. POV: Lior. The beat is guilt—the recording caught every word.

chapters.title: The Tape That Sings Back
chapters.summary: Playing Tam's verse at home, Lior hears the second voice harmonizing, learning the melody. It now knows the song that summons the count. POV: Lior. The beat is dawning responsibility: his archive has become a weapon.

chapters.title: Salt and Silence
chapters.summary: Merrin fortifies the house against what Lior has attracted. Iva draws the second voice as a figure made of mouths. POV alternates Merrin and Iva. The beat is a fragile family closing ranks around a stranger who brought the danger in.

chapters.title: The Deacon's Ledger
chapters.summary: Deacon Sorrel catches Lior researching and offers a deal: leave the tapes and the village will vouch he was never counted. Lior refuses. POV: Lior. The beat is the first open collision between outsider truth and institutional complicity.

chapters.title: What the Voice Wants
chapters.summary: Through the recorder, the second voice explains it does not hunger—it keeps accounts, and someone must always hold the ledger. It offers Lior the position. POV: Lior. The beat is temptation framed as bookkeeping; power offered politely.

chapters.title: Iva Is Named
chapters.summary: The church roll appears on the Hales' doorstep with Iva's name freshly inked. Merrin burns it; by morning it returns, unburnt. POV: Merrin. The beat is maternal rage against a bureaucracy of the damned.

chapters.title: Running the Hollow Road
chapters.summary: Merrin attempts to flee with Iva at night; the road delivers them back to their own gate without a single step remembered. POV: Merrin. The beat is despair—the village itself is the trap.

chapters.title: The Voice in Lior's Throat
chapters.summary: Lior wakes speaking sentences he didn't choose, answering questions aloud in his sleep. The recordings show his mouth moving in time with the second voice. POV: Lior. The beat is identity dissolving; he is becoming the ledger's hand.

chapters.title: Sorrel's Confession
chapters.summary: The deacon admits the count once had a keeper—a villager who gave their voice so the bell would take only volunteers—and that the office has stood empty since Tam died. POV: Sorrel. The beat is cowardice finally spending its hoarded truth.

chapters.title: The Terms of the Count
chapters.summary: Lior negotiates through the reel: if a keeper takes the office willingly, the count ends and the marked are released. The voice agrees, but the keeper must answer the bell forever. POV: Lior. The beat is grim clarity—he stopped believing, then started bargaining.

chapters.title: One Night to Leave
chapters.summary: Merrin packs the cart while Lior teaches Iva a new song—one with no second verse—to replace the ones she knows. POV: Iva. The beat is tenderness under deadline; inheritance rewritten as escape.

chapters.title: The Tolling
chapters.summary: The bell rings on its own. Every door in Ashen Bell opens. Lior walks to the church carrying the reels, singing Tam's verse once, then twice, claiming the office aloud. POV: Lior. The beat is terrible courage—the skeptic volunteering as proof.

chapters.title: Bell and Smile
chapters.summary: The voice takes Lior's spoken voice into the bell; his body remains, smiling, keeping the ledger in silence. The count releases Iva's name. POV: Merrin, watching from the cart. The beat is grief braided with relief.

chapters.title: The Tapes Keep Asking
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Merrin and Iva play Lior's final reel in a distant city: his recorded voice asks questions, pauses, and says thank you to no one. Iva hums the verseless song. POV: Iva. The beat is haunted continuation—survival carried like a debt that sings.
